title: Capstone: design your own agent
description: The course finale: a five-question checklist for designing any agent — goal, tools, pattern, memory, testing.

steps.text: The finale. You've come all the way from tokens to agent swarms. What's left is to pull it together into a working framework — a checklist of five questions for designing any agent. Whether you write code or hire someone to build it, the questions are the same.

steps.imagePrompt: Top-down view of an architect's desk with a blueprint of a small friendly robot. Around the robot on the blueprint, five simple icons: a target, a toolbox, a looping arrow, a memory box and a checkmark. Pencils and a ruler lie nearby.
steps.caption: Five questions — the framework for any agent

steps.question: You know about tools, memory, modes and hooks one by one. Where do you start when you design an agent from scratch?
steps.answer: Not with the model and not with the tools — with the goal. Until you've said what the agent does and how you'll know it worked, the other decisions have nothing to stand on. After that come the five questions, in order.

steps.text: Question 1 — the goal. What should the agent do, and how will you know it worked? One clear task (“I track expenses”) beats “help with everything.” A vague goal is the main reason agents end up useless.

Question 2 — the tools. What does the agent need to touch: files, a calendar, a database, the internet, notifications? Remember the lesson “Agent tools”: an agent is its tools. A few tools with clear descriptions beat a pile of everything thrown together.

Question 3 — the pattern. The task repeats the same way → a workflow or a chain. Requests need sorting → routing. The plan isn't known in advance → an agent with a ReAct loop. Complex and risky → add plan mode with approval. Scale → a swarm.

Question 4 — memory. What should the agent remember between sessions: your profile, facts, a history of actions? Just as important: what must it never store? Remember: everything in the context goes to the model provider.

Question 5 — quality checks. Prepare a dozen typical tasks and run the agent through them after every change. You can judge the results yourself or bring in a judge model — like in the arena. Without such a set you won't know whether things got better or worse: improvements turn into guesswork.

steps.caption: Pick an idea and answer the five questions — the agent card fills in, and mismatches light up

steps.instruction: What does each question of the framework decide?

pairs.def: what the agent does and how to tell it worked
what it's allowed to reach at all
rails, a driver or a mix of both
what to remember between sessions — and what not to keep
how to know a change made things better

steps.text: Bonus technique: structured output. If the agent's answer is read by a program rather than a person, ask for JSON instead of free text. This app works exactly that way: the model returns the chat cards as JSON, and the interface draws them.

steps.situation: Your expense-tracking agent works, but once a week it mixes up categories. You tweak its instructions.
steps.q: How do you tell whether the fix helped?
options: Run a dozen typical messages before and after the fix and compare
Ask the agent itself whether things are clearer for it now
Switch to a smarter model — it will make fewer mistakes anyway
steps.explain: Without a set of typical tasks you're comparing impressions, not results. That's exactly why the testing question sits in the framework right next to the goal and the tools.

steps.text: A common myth: “a good agent = the smartest model.” Not so. More often it comes down to the tools, the pre-prompt and quality checks. No model can rescue a weak design, while a well-thought-out agent works great even on an average one.

steps.instruction: Put the five framework questions in the order you answer them:
items: Memory: what to remember between sessions
Goal: what it does and how to tell it worked
Testing: a set of typical tasks
Pattern: workflow, agent or a mix
steps.explain: The goal comes first — otherwise there's nothing to build the rest on. Then tools and pattern, then memory, and finally whatever you'll measure the result with.

parts.note: tick the tools it needs, a few at most

steps.text: Practice. On paper, design an agent for your own life using the five questions. For example, an “expense agent”: goal — tracking spending; tools — a database and notifications; pattern — a workflow with an agent inside; memory — categories and limits; testing — 10 typical messages like “spent $5 on coffee.” Then build it: the “Open the builder” button at the end of the lesson opens a chat with Builder, a built-in agent. Answer its questions and tick the boxes on its cards using your five answers. When the draft is ready, tap “Review your agent”: the review screen shows everything at once, lets you change any part, and is where you publish. Prefer a form? “Edit step by step” on that screen opens it.

In short. The agent framework: goal → tools → pattern → memory → testing. Go through the five questions — and you have a design. Congratulations: you've reached the end of the course, and now you think like an agent builder, not just a user.

questions.q: Which question does agent design start with?
options: Goal: what it does and how to tell it worked
Picking the most expensive, smartest model
Designing the icon and a catchy name
questions.explain: A clear goal comes first — without it, the other decisions have nothing to stand on.

questions.q: Why do you need a set of test tasks?
options: To see after each change whether it got better or worse
To train the model on those very tasks
To show the client a nice table of numbers
questions.explain: Running typical tasks is the only way to measure quality instead of guessing.

questions.q: What most often decides an agent's quality?
options: Tools, pre-prompt and testing — not just the model
Only the size and price of the chosen model
The length and detail of the system prompt
questions.explain: Agent design matters more than the model's “smarts”: a well-designed agent works even on an average model.
